title: Question 1: Expanding the Public Records Law

context.text: Placed on the ballot by initiative petition: the Information for Voters labels it a law proposed by initiative petition on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026. The Legislature's Special Joint Committee on Initiative Petitions issued the legislative reports reproduced in the same booklet.

question.text: Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? Expanding the Public Records Law: This proposed law would make most records held by the Legislature and the Office of the Governor public records under the Massachusetts Public Records Law. This proposed law would exempt documents related to the development of public policy and communications between legislators and their constituents, if those communications are reasonably related to a constituent’s request for assistance in obtaining government-provided benefits or services or interacting with a government agency.

summary.text: The measure would make most records held by the Legislature and the Office of the Governor public records under the Massachusetts Public Records Law, while exempting documents related to the development of public policy and communications between legislators and their constituents that are reasonably related to a constituent's request for assistance in obtaining government benefits or services or dealing with a government agency. Statement of fiscal consequences (Executive Office for Administration and Finance): The proposed law has no discernible material fiscal consequences for state and municipal government finances.

measure.yesMeans: A YES VOTE would make most records held by the Legislature and the Office of the Governor public records under the Massachusetts Public Records Law.
measure.noMeans: A NO VOTE would make no change to the Massachusetts Public Records Law.

argumentsFor.text: In the 150-word argument in favor signed by Diana DiZoglio of the Committee for Transparency and Democracy, as printed in the Information for Voters: "Massachusetts deserves open government. Good government groups rank our state the least transparent in the nation. We’re one of only two states where both the Governor’s office and the Legislature claim a blanket exemption from the public records law."

sources.title: 2026 Massachusetts Information for Voters (State Election, November 3, 2026)
sources.publisher: Secretary of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts

researchNotes: Ballot text, official yes/no statements and fiscal statements are taken from the Secretary of the Commonwealth's 2026 Information for Voters booklet (PDF text extracted and checked by script). Arguments are quoted from the signed 150-word pro/con statements, which the Commonwealth states reflect the authors' opinions and are not certified as accurate. No signed argument against appears: the booklet states there was no organized group urging a No vote and prints text compiled by the Secretary's office, which is not quoted here. The booklet's own summary is the Attorney General's; the Secretary's page and Ballotpedia could not be fetched (bot protection), so the ballot list was confirmed from the booklet itself, which covers nine questions.
